absaetze.t: Le 16 novembre, les chefs d’États et gouvernements de l'Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) pourraient élire au Cambodge leur secrétaire général par un vote, une première. Entre rivalité RDC-Rwanda, guerre d'influence et critiques en interne sur le bilan de la sortante, rarement la course aura été aussi serrée.
5 min Temps de lecture
De notre envoyé spécial à Phnom Penh,

Sur la route de l’aéroport, la capitale cambodgienne a hissé les couleurs de la Francophonie. Le long du boulevard Hun Sen - du nom de l’ex-Premier ministre et actuel homme fort du pays -, le thème du XXe sommet s’affiche en français et en khmer : « Réinvestir dans la paix pour une prospérité partagée et une stabilité durable ». Mais plus que l’avenir d’une organisation exposée aux fractures du multilatéralisme et fragilisée financièrement, dans les délégations c’est la succession de Louise Mushikiwabo qui domine les débats.

La nouveauté tient d’abord à la procédure. Le règlement adopté à Djerba en 2022, garde le consensus comme mode de désignation, mais ouvre une porte : à défaut d’entente, les chefs d’États et de gouvernement des 53 pays membres voteront à la majorité simple. Dans l'hypothèse d'un scrutin serré, 14 voix pourraient suffire à l'emporter. « Un secrétaire général élu par une minorité d’États n’aurait aucune légitimité, redoute-t-on en interne. Ce serait mortifère pour l’organisation. »
Une sortante et trois prétendants

Dans cette course à quatre, la sortante Louise Mushikiwabo se présente pour un troisième mandat. La Rwandaise, ex-cheffe de la diplomatie de son pays s’appuie sur son solide réseau diplomatique pour rallier des soutiens et défend son bilan : modernisation de l’institution et recentrage sur quelques programmes phares : le numérique, l’entrepreneuriat des femmes et la formation des jeunes.

Face à elle, la Congolaise Juliana Amato Lumumba, plaide pour une « Francophonie des peuples » centrée sur la dignité du sud global. L’ancienne ministre de la Culture de son pays joue par ailleurs sur un nom qui porte : celui de son père, Patrice Lumumba, figure fondatrice de la RDC et icône du panafricanisme.

Restent deux autres concurrents : le Roumain Dacian Cioloș - ancien Premier ministre et ex-commissaire européen à l’agriculture - a fait campagne sur une Francophonie des « opportunités » tournée vers l’économie, quand la Mauritanienne Coumba Bâ, médecin et ancienne ministre de son pays, se présente comme la candidate du rassemblement, capable d’incarner la solution de compromis africaine.
Le conflit RDC/Rwanda dans la campagne

Plus que les idées, c’est le conflit entre Kinshasa et Kigali qui s’est imposé dans la campagne. En coulisse, la RDC, qui accuse le Rwanda de soutenir les rebelles du M23, s’active pour empêcher la réélection de la Rwandaise. Au point de menacer de quitter l’OIF en cas de victoire de Louise Mushikiwabo.

La RDC ne brandit pas l’avertissement publiquement, mais sur RFI, le ministre congolais de la Communication, Patrick Muyaya, déclare le 11 novembre : « Si le choix qui est fait à Phnom Penh ne reflète pas les valeurs que nous portons, nous en tirerons les conséquences ».
À écouter aussiOIF: «La réélection de Louise Mushikiwabo ne correspondrait pas à nos valeurs», déclare le porte-parole de la RDC, Patrick Muyaya

D’après plusieurs sources recueillies par RFI, la RDC menace de frapper vite et fort. La rupture du Congo avec l’OIF pourrait être annoncée dès l’issue du huis clos de Phnom Penh le 16 novembre, ou dans les jours qui suivent à Kinshasa. « La guerre entre les deux pays n’est pas que verbale, analyse sur notre antenne Francis Kpatindé enseignant-chercheur à Sciences Po Paris. Si la RDC, premier pays locuteurs francophone (avec 57 millions de personnes), se retire de l’organisation, ça en sera fini de l’OIF. »
L’OIF détournée au profit du Rwanda ?

Louise Mushikiwabo n’est pas seulement attaquée depuis Kinshasa. Au siège parisien de l’institution, certains l’accusent de passivité sur l’invasion russe de l’Ukraine en 2022 comme sur le retrait du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger de l’OIF en mars 2025. A l’inverse, elle est présentée comme particulièrement active sur des dossiers chers à Kigali : du soutien au président Mamadi Doumbouya en Guinée à la réélection du chef de l’État centrafricain Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

De quoi faire naitre des soupçons d’une organisation détournée au profit du Rwanda ? « Ces missions font partie du travail de médiation de l’OIF », répond l’entourage de la candidate. « Il y a un pro-activisme troublant », rétorque pourtant un fonctionnaire.

Autre reproche fait à la Rwandaise : son management vertical. « Asservir l’OIF aux intérêts de Paul Kagame implique une approche brutale et une mise au pas de l’organisation », affirme ce même fonctionnaire qui dit avoir vu des collègues licenciés ou relégués à des postes subalternes.

« On ne fait jamais l’unanimité en politique », balaye la porte-parole de l’OIF, Oria Vande Weghe qui préfère souligner « les réformes engagées depuis 2018, à commencer par la mise en place d’une procédure claire pour l’élection du secrétaire générale. Louise Mushikiwabo ne s’excusera jamais d’avoir apporté de la rigueur, et mené des réformes », ajoute-t-elle.
Le candidat roumain en alternative

Les critiques contre la sortante, ajoutées aux tensions entre Kigali et Kinshasa, pourraient profiter au Roumain Dacian Cioloș. La RDC n’exclurait pas de lui apporter son soutien si sa candidate venait à être mise hors-jeu. « Le seul défaut de Dacian Cioloș, confie un connaisseur, c'est qu'il n'est pas Africain. » Un obstacle de taille quand on sait que le continent concentre 26 des 53 membres et 65 % des francophones.

A cinq jours du huis clos de Phnom Penh, rien ne semble joué. Lors du dernier Conseil européen, Emmanuel Macron a rencontré le candidat roumain en tête à tête. Pas de quoi faire de l’entrevue un soutien officiel de Paris qui n’a pas communiqué sa position, mais dans la dernière ligne droite, chacun en vient à scruter les moindres signaux.

items.titel: Netanyahu fights to stay relevant as Israel’s opposition closes in
items.anriss: A new Knesset shaped by October 7 prepares to convene as Netanyahu fights to prevent an opposition-led government

absaetze.t: In the last few days, in marked contrast to an election campaign defined by its bitterness and the closeness of its personal attacks, Israel’s current prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken of national unity and coming together with the opposition bloc that edged out his ruling coalition in October’s election.

On Saturday, the same day that Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government capable of commanding the Knesset, Netanyahu published a video on his social media account claiming Israel to be facing the genuine risk of civil war if a government were established with the support of Arab parties which he accused of wanting to “eliminate the State of Israel”.

Two days later, Netanyahu returned to the theme of existential threat in a further video, calling upon the leaders of the more successful bloc to recognise the “needs of the hour” and join, under his leadership, a single unified government that would also include the ultra-Orthodox parties, at least one of which is understood to be in talks with Eisenkot, as well as the prime minister’s controversial allies on the far right, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir.

“It’s all a game at the moment. It’s leverage, it’s one-upmanship, it’s psyops, it’s spin, it’s counter-spin,” former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy said of the invariably long and complex negotiations that take place ahead of establishing a government,

Currently, with the new Knesset being sworn in on Tuesday, speculation is focussing on the role of the Ultra Orthodox, or haredim, parties, which have traditionally offered support to Netanyahu in return for measures shielding their young male yeshiva students from the military draft in defiance off a Super Court ruling of June 2024.
Strategy

Nevertheless, irrespective of the past political cover offered to their members by Netanyahu, there are suggestions that one of the Ultra Orthodox parties United Torah Judaism (UTJ) – which refused to endorse Netanyahu’s selection to build a government by the President – is preparing to throw in behind Eisenkot, with the objections of one of the opposition’s principal figures Avigdor Lieberman said to be quieted in the face of either partnering with one of the Arab parties or the continued rule of Lieberman’s nemesis, Netanyahu and the prospect of further elections.

“‘It’s political strategy, that’s all,” Netanyahu’s former aide, Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak said from Jerusalem. ‘But he’s negotiating from a weakened position. With the UTJ, Eisenkot’s got 67 seats,’ he said of the numbers needed to gain a working majority in the 120 seat Knesset, “so, of course, Netanyahu’s going to do all he can to reinforce his bloc; Barak said of negotiations regarded by many as critical to Netanyahu’s personal future.
Netanyahu faces a number of challenges that speak directly to both his political legacy and personal freedom that he will lose all influence over should Eisenkot succeed him.

Foremost are like to be the multiple corruption charges that is is presently on trial for and, despite his claims of innocence that he has already preemptively petitioned the country’s President and his former political rival, Isaac Herzog for. Secondly, and more pressingly is the question of his and his government’s culpability for the alleged failings ahead of the October 7 Hamas led attack that triggered the genocide unleashed upon Gaza by Israel and the multiple strikes and attacks launched by Israel non regional neighbors in the years since.
New Knesset, new danger

Many of the new MKs being sworn in on Tuesday, including bereaved family members, reservists, advocates for the 250 or so Israelis taken captive that day and Eisenkot himself, who lost a son and two nephews in the genocide that followed, are all tied directly to October 7 and the wars that followed together creating a chamber where feelings over the October 7 attack and where culpability for its lies are said to run close to the surface.

In particular, attention is likely to focus sharply on Netanyahu himself, whose supposed miscalculations ahead of the attack, stories of numerous missed warnings and who was subsequently accused of dragging out the war, or sacrificing the welfare off the captives for his own political ends. Key among the opposition’s aims for the first day of parliamentary business is set to be the installation of Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar (“straight”) party and a keen advocate of a state inquiry into Netanyahu and the government’s failings ahead of the Hamas led attack.

“Having so many people connected so directly to October 7 is going to increase the temperature, but it’s become so politicized that a win for one side automatically becomes a loss for the other, so the bereaved family on the right can say we need to increase our militarism in honor of my son, and the bereaved family in the center says we need to enlist more people.
“Netanyahu can try to influence that but for the first time in a long time, he seems a bit lost,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg said.

However, how lost Netanyahu may be, or how grounded his claims of pending civil war or destruction at the hands of regional adversaries may be, ultimately, his political and potentially personal fate now lies with an opposition that outstrips his own numerically and a volatile Knesset eager to comb over the mistakes of the past.
“There’s no appetite on the other side to go in with Netanyahu for a unity government,” Levy said,

“The only real circumstances under which that happen is if he can create a security emergency,” he said following a weekend where the UK press had reported daily phone calls from Netanyahu to the Trump administration urging renewed war on Iran.

items.titel: Markets fluctuate as US rate worries temper tech bounce
items.anriss: Ahead of European markets opening on Wednesday, Asian stocks diverged as renewed optimism over the AI trade was offset by forecast-topping US inflation data and the prospect of a bumper interest rate hike next month.

absaetze.t: After last week's rout, fuelled by fears that Democrats would ramp up regulation of artificial intelligence, beaten-down tech stocks have bounced this week on bargain-buying and a feeling that their fears may have been overdone.
ADVERTISEMENT
Sentiment was also given a boost by earnings from data centre operator CoreWeave, which said sales would come in at $13-13.3 billion (€11.6-11.9bn) this year, beating estimates.

The news soothed worries about the company's health after it suffered heavy selling last month amid speculation that it could struggle to finance its vast debt pile as borrowing costs continued to rise.
That sparked a period of panic over the tech sector as firms rely heavily on debt to fund their eye-watering AI investments.
Also lifting confidence was Anthropic's filing showing it planned to raise up to $64 billion (€57.1bn) in its upcoming initial public offering, valuing it at as much as $1.4 trillion (€1.25trn).
The maker of AI agent Claude had been expected to raise up to $100 billion (€89.2bn) in its IPO, which would have made it the largest IPO on record.
The stock market debut is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom can last.
Its filing also revealed that revenue soared to $17 billion (€15.2bn) in the third quarter, up from just $1.4 billion (€1.25bn) a year earlier.

And in another sign of the sector's health, Bloomberg reported that ChatGPT-maker OpenAI had earned $10 billion (€8.92bn) in quarterly revenue for the first time in July-September, thanks to demand for its software.
The figure marked an increase of nearly 50% from the previous three months and a near threefold jump year on year.
However, chip giant Nvidia was still in focus following the bombshell revelation of an affair between CEO Jensen Huang and a woman reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The firm is now the subject of an FBI investigation.
'No shortage of catalysts'
All three main indexes on Wall Street ended in the red on Tuesday, snapping a two-day rally, while Asian markets stuttered.
Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei – where most of Asia's leading AI-linked firms are listed – continued to rise, with Singapore and Jakarta also up.
But there were losses in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Wellington and Manila.
Traders are also now fretting over the possibility of a bigger-than-expected interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve when it next meets in December.
US consumer prices rose 0.4% month on month in October, a slowdown from the previous month's 0.6% but more than the 0.3% forecast.
While the reading reflected a significant moderation in energy price increases, food prices shot higher, along with medical care, household furnishings and several other categories.
Chicago Fed boss Austan Goolsbee told PBS NewsHour the reading was "another distressing report, borderline disturbing".
The report came hours after Fed Governor Christopher Waller called for a swift response to inflation, suggesting he could even support a 50-basis-point hike in December.
A second Fed official, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, also signalled strong support for swift action to address inflation.
"Market participants continue to navigate the political implications of the Democratic sweep, and the economics of AI infrastructure," said Pepperstone's Chris Weston.
He said investors were "forced to reassess assumptions around future revenues, cash flows and funding conditions".

"Add a hotter-than-expected US (consumer price) print, a heightened focus on Anthropic's IPO, and a major buyers' strike on Nvidia, and there's no shortage of catalysts driving market price action," he added.
Oil prices edged up after sinking again on Tuesday on hopes for a US-Iran agreement to end their war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
International benchmark Brent was hovering around $92 (€82.06) a barrel, after dropping below $90 (€80.28) for the first time since August.
Both contracts are down around 20% since the start of the month.
In company news, Japanese tech investment giant SoftBank tumbled as much as 8% in Tokyo after reporting a more than $7 billion (€6.24bn) loss in the fiscal second quarter.

items.titel: For diabetes patients, stopping GLP-1 drugs linked to doubled risk of heart attack, stroke, death
items.anriss: People with type 2 diabetes who stopped GLP-1 treatment had twice the risk of heart attack, stroke or death than those who continued, according to a new study.

absaetze.t: Published on 11 November 2026 - 7:13 GMT+1

Breakthrough medicines used for cutting weight and addressing diabetes mimic the natural GLP-1 hormone to regulate blood sugar and curb appetite. In recent years, they have become a cornerstone of treatment for type 2 diabetes and obesity, also showing benefits for heart and kidney health.
ADVERTISEMENT

Despite their proven effects, a substantial proportion of patients stop taking these drugs, often within the first year. Common reasons include gastrointestinal side effects, perceived lack of efficacy, high costs, and concern about rare side effects.
Coming off treatment is frequently followed by weight regain and a worsening of several cardiometabolic risk factors, such as blood sugar and blood pressure.

Now, a new study, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe, found that stopping such medicines was linked to a doubled combined risk of non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, or death from any cause compared to those who continued. This equates to roughly four events per 100 people per year among those who stopped, compared with two per 100 among those who continued.

Among those who stopped treatment, the risks were higher for people with obesity than for those without. People with obesity (a body mass index above 30) had a 127% higher cardiovascular risk after coming off GLP-1s, compared with a 61% increase among those without obesity.
However, because it was an observational study, it cannot determine whether discontinuing GLP-1s directly causes the increased risk or whether people who stopped were already in poorer health.

After people stopped treatment, their weight, blood sugar and blood pressure changed only slightly, and there were no significant differences between those who suffered a heart attack, stroke or death and those who didn’t. This suggests these factors may not fully explain the higher risk, the authors noted.

The researchers analysed electronic medical records from more than 300 diabetes clinics in the Italian Association of Clinical Diabetologists database. The records covered over 80,000 people with type 2 diabetes and no established cardiovascular disease who had started a GLP-1 between 2004 and 2024.

The majority of participants received earlier-generation GLP-1s. Semaglutide — one of the most common new-generation treatments — accounted for only a minor fraction of use, and tirzepatide was not included because it entered the Italian market after the study period.
People who continued treatment took a GLP-1 for nearly three years on average, compared with just over one year for those who stopped.

The authors say the findings suggest that, in people with type 2 diabetes and no established cardiovascular disease, long-term GLP-1 use may be important for maintaining overall health benefits. They noted that further research is needed to determine whether stopping directly contributes to increased cardiovascular risk or is instead a marker of worsening health or underlying cardiovascular risk.

items.titel: Army Wants New Palletized Short-Range Air Defenses In Service By The End Of 2029
items.anriss: The U.S. Army is aiming to have new palletized short-range air defense systems in service before the 2029 calendar year comes to a close. The service expects these systems to be fielded on crewed and uncrewed vehicles, as well as deployed …

absaetze.t: The U.S. Army is aiming to have new palletized short-range air defense systems in service before the 2029 calendar year comes to a close. The service expects these systems to be fielded on crewed and uncrewed vehicles, as well as deployed in static positions. The goal is to give combat units a more flexible array of point defenses against aerial threats, especially drone swarms, but it could also be used against ground targets.

New details about what the Army formally calls the Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense Increment 4 (M-SHORAD Inc 4) program are included in briefing slides recently released online. The presentation was originally produced for an industry day event held in Huntsville, Alabama, last month.

The overarching M-SHORAD program traces back to the late 2010s. Increment 1 produced a new mobile short-range air defense system based on the Stryker 8×8 light armored vehicle, which is now called the Sgt. Stout.

Increment 2 has been focused on operationalizing counter-drone directed energy weapons, and laser-based designs in particular. Increment 3 was originally centered on the Next Generation Short-Range Interceptor (NGSRI), a replacement for the venerable Stinger short-range surface-to-air missile. It also now covers work on the 30mm XM1223 Multi-Mode Proximity Airburst (MMPA) round for use in ground vehicles armed with the M914 cannon, like the Sgt. Stout. Development of another 30mm airburst round for use in the M230 cannons on AH-64 Apache attack helicopters falls outside of the M-SHORAD umbrella.

Increment 4 first emerged in 2025. The Army previously said it was looking for systems that could reasonably be fielded sometime between Fiscal Years 2027 and 2029. Schedule layouts in the newly released briefing slides show the goal now is to reach Initial Operational Capability (IOC) in Fiscal Year 2030. More specifically, the Army wants to hit the First Unit Equipped (FUE) milestone with a battalion-sized element in the first quarter of the 2030 fiscal cycle, which runs from October 1 to December 31 of 2029.

The Army wants the Increment 4 system to be capable of defeating a wide range of uncrewed aerial systems, from small quadcopters up to longer-range one-way-attack drones like Iran’s Shahed 136, operating individually or in swarms. It also has to be able to provide point defense against traditional helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft making attack runs on friendly ground units. The newly released briefing explicitly highlights a secondary “direct fire capability for ground targets,” as well.

No mention is made of cruise missile threats, which the Army is currently working to address through other air defense systems. However, it is possible that future M-SHORAD Increment 4 systems could be able to engage lower-end cruise missiles in certain flight profiles.

Increment 4 systems have to come in a “vehicle-agnostic” palletized format, or what the Army describes as a Self-Loading Equipment Dock (SLED), that can be readily mounted on and dismounted from light vehicles. The service has named its 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTV) and Infantry Squad Vehicles (ISV), as well as uncrewed ground vehicles (UGV), as potential hosts. The Army does not want options that require additional trailers. As palletized systems, they could also be offloaded at forward sites for static point defense.

Regardless of how they are configured, the Army wants the Increment 4 systems to “be able to operate for 72 hours independently, and semi-independently with supported force for 3-7 days,” per the recently released briefing. It also lists “C-130 loadable in normal SLED & vehicle configuration without special equipment; air droppable, sling-load and dismount capable” as key requirements.

When it comes to sensors and effectors for Increment 4, the Army continues to leave the requirements wide open for prospective vendors. The recent briefing simply notes that the systems have to feature a “reconfigurable multi-effector MEP [mission equipment package] integrating kinetic effects (e.g. missiles, direct-fire guns), and non-kinetic defeat.”

Several defense contractors – L3Harris, Leidos, Leonardo DRS, MDH Strategic Services, Moog, MSI Defense Solutions, SAIC, and the Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC), to name a few – have already publicly shown relevant designs. Versions of L3Harris’ VAMPIRE (Vehicle-Agnostic Modular Palletized ISR Rocket Equipment) systems and the Electronic Advanced Ground Launcher System (EAGLS) from MSI are already in at least limited use within the U.S. military. VAMPIRE, as well as the BRAWLR (Battery Revolving Adaptive Weapons Launcher-Reconfigurable) from SNC, are also now combat-proven as a result of service in Ukraine.

Many of the systems highlighted above feature guns like the aforementioned 30mm M914 cannon or 7.62x51mm M134 Miniguns. Stingers and AGM-114 Hellfires are commonly featured interceptors, too. SNC’s BRAWLR, which the company is also pitching for maritime applications, is notably designed to accommodate traditional anti-air missiles like the AIM-9X Sidewinder, as well.

Virtually all of the potential contenders for M-SHORAD Increment 4 incorporate anti-air optimized 70mm laser-guided Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II (APKWS II) rockets. Originally designed as an air-to-ground weapon, APKWS II has now firmly established its place as a lower-cost counter-drone interceptor capable of being used in surface-to-air and air-to-air modes. The Ukrainian military was the first to employ these rockets in combat in the counter-drone role, but they are now in widespread U.S. military use in this capacity, too. A growing number of other countries are now moving to field APKWS II, as well as other similar laser-guided rockets, as anti-air weapons, as well.

Whatever specific types of Increment 4 systems the Army ultimately acquires, the requirement that they be palletized will offer inherent mobility and flexibility, even when not mounted on a particular host vehicle. Those attributes, in turn, could be especially beneficial for future expeditionary or distributed operations.

“Think of like a pallet or a sled that I could put in the back of any vehicle — whether it’s an ISV, a Humvee, a JLTV, or even a technical vehicle like a Toyota truck — and I can have that self-contained capability that allows the maneuver commander to have a menu of options,” then-Army Col. Marc Pelini said about Increment 4 at a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in 2025. “When I talk about [a] menu of options, I’m talking about being able to pull off a radar like an X-band radar and put a Ku-band radar on, or pull a Coyote [counter-drone interceptor] pod off and put a Stinger pod on.”

At the time, Pelini was the military deputy for the Fires Future Capability Directorate within the Army’s Transformation and Training Command (T2COM). Pelini has since been promoted to brigadier general and is now the Army’s top air defense artillery officer.

“And then, as we look at the various capabilities that are out there, from a sensing perspective, you have acoustic sensors, you have bistatic sensors, you have active radar, you have EO/IR [electro-optical/infrared] cameras. So coming up with a way that we can fuse those at the platform and at the tactical edge, and then eventually bring that up into the cloud, where we can do fusion across the entirety of the AOR [area of responsibility],” Pelini added back in 2025. “The system itself, or the pallet itself, recognizes that and automatically changes the user interface for the operator to engage those threats. So the way that we’re taking that is through an open hardware and software – really kind of a plug-and-play approach to it.”

The networking component here is particularly important as it will allow air defenders to employ Increment 4 systems in a more effective manner even if they are dispersed across a broad area. Since the systems may not all be configured in the same way, this will give operators more options to employ the effectors best suited to the incoming threats they are faced with, too. The Army currently has a network designed primarily for use with shorter-range air defense systems called Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control (FAAD C2). The service is in the process now of transitioning to the newer and more expansive Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS) network.

As mentioned at the start of this story, the kind of massed effects and fused capabilities that Increment 4 promises to this overarching architecture is seen as particularly important to helping address large volumes of drones operating in their own networked swarms.

“Right now, there is not one system that’s going to be able to defeat that swarm,” now-retired Lt. Gen. Sean Gainey, then commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC), said during a separate panel at the AUSA conference in 2025.

For a decade now, TWZ has been sounding the alarm on the drone swarm threat, and pointing to deeply layered air defense concepts with mixtures of different effectors and soft-kill systems like electronic warfare jammers as the only way to put up an effective defense. We have drawn attention to this in the past specifically within the context of larger short-range air defense gaps facing the U.S. military. The M-SHORAD effort, overall, has been at the center of Army efforts in recent years to close those gaps.

Increment 4 has always been planned to be just one layer in a still-expanding next-generation Army air defense architecture. The Army is in the process of acquiring a slew of new higher- and lower-end anti-air interceptors, as well as launchers to fire them. Laser and microwave directed energy weapons are also set to be part of this ecosystem. New and improved radars and other sensors are included in this broader air defense modernization push, too.
If the Army’s current plan for Increment 4 holds, the palletized systems will start joining its larger air defense arsenal right before the end of the decade.

items.titel: House Republicans sidestep effort to impeach Hegseth
items.anriss: The House voted Tuesday evening to send the proposed impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively quashing an effort to oust Hegseth from his cabinet post.

absaetze.t: The House voted Tuesday evening to send the proposed impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively quashing an effort to oust Hegseth from his cabinet post.

In a 211 to 204 vote, House Republicans sidestepped an effort proposed by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach Hegseth. Massie charged that Hegseth was negligent and conducted illegal activity in his handling of counternarcotics operations and extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and Pacific; attacking Iran in February without congressional approval; retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for the veteran lawmaker’s statements to troops on illegal orders; capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro without a declaration of war; and other operations.

“Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” the articles stated.
The decision to send the articles to the Judiciary Committee likely delays the vote until January, when Democrats take over the majority in Congress.
As of Thursday, Democrats won 256 seats in the House to the Republicans’ 168, while in the Senate, Democrats have at least 54 seats to 44 Republican seats.
If the House votes to impeach Hegseth next year, a two-thirds majority would be needed on any of the articles to force Hegseth out of office.

In a rare news conference Tuesday morning before the vote, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” seeking to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”
Noting that President Donald Trump was impeached twice but not convicted, Hegseth said he would “take that company every day of the week.”
“These resolutions are a farce. They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders,” Hegseth said.
Trump has said he would stand by his defense secretary, saying Monday that he’s “done a very good job.”

If the effort had succeeded, it would have marked the second impeachment of a U.S. defense secretary and third of a cabinet member. In 2024, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over President Joe Biden’s immigration policies at the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate voted to dismiss the charges before it went to trial.
Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 on corruption charges shortly after he resigned. He was later acquitted in the Senate.

A survey released in October by the military-veterans advocacy non-profit Common Defense found that troops and family members are uncomfortable with what they see as the politicization of the armed forces.
According to the survey, conducted by Change Research, 54% of active-duty personnel surveyed disapproved of Hegseth, while 64% of military family members disapproved.

A majority of the group of 731 active-duty troops, veterans and military family members also believe decisions within the department were being made for political gain, and 53% of active-duty personnel said the politicization was making them want to leave the military sooner than anticipated.
Nearly half the active-duty personnel also said they oppose Operation Epic Fury, the United States’ operation against Iran.

items.titel: « Le regard sur le béton commence à changer » : comment la France apprend à restaurer son patrimoine du XXe siècle
items.anriss: Si la tour Perret à Grenoble, œuvre en béton armé d’Auguste Perret, est connue aux États-Unis et au Japon, elle l’est moins dans la patrie du célèbre architecte. Et pour cause, jusqu’à l’inscription en 2005 sur la liste du Patrimoine …

absaetze.t: Le patrimoine du XXe siècle regroupe une grande diversité de bâtiments construits avec des matériaux qui se sont révélés moins durables que ceux du passé. Le béton, en particulier, pose des problématiques spécifiques.

Si la tour Perret à Grenoble, œuvre en béton armé d’Auguste Perret, est connue aux États-Unis et au Japon, elle l’est moins dans la patrie du célèbre architecte. Et pour cause, jusqu’à l’inscription en 2005 sur la liste du Patrimoine mondial de l’Unesco du centre-ville du Havre reconstruit par Perret, le béton a plus souvent été considéré comme un matériau fonctionnel que patrimonial. Fermée dans les années 1960, cette tour d’observation érigée en 1925 présentait d’importants signes d’altération du béton et une corrosion des armatures en acier.
Le dilemme de la tour Perret : Intervention minimum, protection maximum

Face à l’ampleur des dégradations, l’architecte en chef des Monuments historiques François Botton a proposé une tranche d’essais grandeur nature afin de tester plusieurs techniques de restauration. « Nous étions face à un nœud gordien : réaliser le minimum d’interventions sur la matière d’origine, un béton des années 1920 acide et poreux qui génère des pathologies, et le maximum d’interventions pour la pérennité de l’œuvre », explique l’architecte Cédric Avenier, membre du comité scientifique de la restauration de la tour Perret à Grenoble et expert ICOMOS spécialisé dans l’architecture du XXe siècle et les bétons patrimoniaux. Avant de poursuivre : « Pour les huit piliers principaux, nous avons utilisé du béton projeté, technique utilisée pour restaurer les tunnels et stabiliser les falaises. Nous avons mis au point un béton spécifique, comprenant des granulats et un ciment, compatibles avec le matériau de 1925 au niveau technique et esthétique. »
Achevée en 1925 et fermée depuis 1965, la tour Perret, à Grenoble, a rouvert au public le 10 juillet 2026. ©Thierry Chenu – Ville De Grenoble.
Le béton, armature du XXe siècle en danger

Le Laboratoire de recherche des monuments historiques (LRMH) mène depuis 1993 des recherches sur le patrimoine en béton. Parmi ses sujets d’études, l’identification des pathologies spécifiques, le développement d’outils de diagnostic et le traitement en restauration et conservation. « Le regard sur le béton commence à changer parce qu’il est aujourd’hui possible de réaliser de belles restaurations durables comme celles de l’église Notre-Dame du Raincy ou du Palais d’Iéna, dont la restauration des façades a été récompensée par l’American Concrete Institute », se réjouit Elisabeth Marie-Victoire, responsable du pôle scientifique Béton au sein du LRMH. Conscient que la restauration des bétons anciens exige des savoir-faire et connaissances techniques très spécifiques, le Groupement des entreprises de restauration de Monuments historiques a œuvré à la publication d’un guide intitulé Les Bétons du patrimoine.
Entièrement reconstruite à l’identique, la Maison de fer, à Poissy, a été inaugurée en 2020. ©Ville de Poissy.

Le syndicat professionnel a également été partie prenante dans l’élaboration de deux nouvelles qualifications Qualibat attestant de compétences techniques en restauration des bétons du patrimoine. H. Chevalier fait partie des entreprises qui détiennent ces savoir-faire particuliers. Parmi ses chantiers, on peut citer le théâtre des Champs-Élysées à Paris et la réhabilitation de l’ancien pavillon des femmes du sanatorium d’Aincourt, dans le Val-d’Oise. Construit entre 1931 et 1933, cet édifice, à l’abandon depuis 2001, était en piteux état. « Nous avons analysé mécaniquement et chimiquement la nature des bétons et des fers ainsi que l’état de la structure. L’objectif était de conserver l’aspect d’origine des façades et le principe de circulation intérieure », explique Riccardo Giordano, architecte en chef des Monuments historiques. Plusieurs années de travail ont été nécessaires pour transformer ce bâtiment en logements. « Nous avons nettoyé, brossé, purgé les bétons abîmés, changé les fers pourris avant d’appliquer un produit spécial pour protéger les nouveaux fers de la rouille puis un mortier de réparation », résume Mohamed Rahmani, chef de chantier chez H. Chevalier.
l’ancien pavillon des femmes du sanatorium d’Aincourt, dans le Val-d’Oise, à l’abandon. ©Antoine Mercusot.

Un label dédié pour les oeuvres de moins de cent ans Le label « Architecture contemporaine remarquable », qui remplace depuis 2016 le label « Patrimoine du XXe siècle », signale les édifices et productions de moins de cent ans non protégés au titre des Monuments historiques. Parmi les critères d’éligibilité, on peut citer la singularité de l’œuvre et le caractère innovant ou expérimental de la conception architecturale, urbaine, paysagère ou de la réalisation technique. À ce jour, 1 392 immeubles, ensembles architecturaux, ouvrages d’art et aménagements sont labellisés. M. L.
Du métal au plastique, autant de problématiques de conservation

À Poissy, dans les Yvelines, la Maison de fer, maison en kit imaginée par l’ingénieur Joseph Danly en 1896, doit son nom au matériau qui la constitue. « Suite à la tempête de 1999, la maison n’était plus qu’un amas de tôles au milieu d’un terrain de ronces. Les services techniques de la ville les ont récupérées et triées et le maire a souhaité que la maison soit reconstruite à l’identique dans le parc Meissonier », raconte Philippe Blanc, architecte en charge de la restauration de cet édifice atypique, inscrit à l’inventaire supplémentaire des Monuments historiques depuis 1975. Certaines tôles ont pu être restaurées, d’autres réutilisées et plus de la moitié ont été fabriquées avant d’être assemblées tel un puzzle.
Les tuyaux de la façade du Centre Pompidou côté rue du Renard et détail de la corrosion de sa structure métallique. ©Aia Life Designers Architecture, ADAGP, 2026.

Ovni architectural ayant suscité de nombreuses controverses lors de sa construction, le Centre Pompidou, qui sera prochainement inscrit au titre des Monuments historiques, fait actuellement l’objet d’une rénovation d’ampleur. « Outre la mise aux normes énergétiques, il y a un enjeu très fort : l’amiante. Nous allons remplacer l’intégralité des façades dont celles situées rue du Renard, composées de plaques d’amiante-ciment. Par ailleurs, les vitrages sont endommagés et doivent être remplacés pour assurer la sécurité des personnes, notamment en situation d’incendie », énumère l’architecte Adrien Paporello, directeur d’Agence chez AIA Life Designers. D’autres matériaux (lamellé-collé, plastique…) inventés au XXe siècle poseront aussi des problèmes d’entretien et de conservation dans les prochaines décennies. S’ouvre ici un champ nouveau pour les entreprises et les laboratoires de recherche.

items.titel: Caá Porá Arquitectura and Jerome Haferd Studio design drum-like performance centre for Ecuador
items.anriss: Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador , with a central venue that has massive bamboo support …

absaetze.t: Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador, with a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.
The campus includes dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.
Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.
Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.
“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.
“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”
“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”
The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.
These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.
Acoustin fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.
A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back of house facilities.
An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.
As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.
These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” said the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.
The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

items.titel: Knocking on heaven’s door: Will the Pope make ‘God’s architect’ Antoni Gaudí a saint?
items.anriss: In April 2025, the celebrated Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí took the first steps towards becoming a saint when the Vatican announced that Pope Francis had authorised a decree declaring him “venerable”. Next up: beatification. Now at this …

absaetze.t: Design
November 11, 2026
2 Min Read
The Vatican has put Gaudí on a path to sainthood. But would the architect want that? Heaven only knows.

In April 2025, the celebrated Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí took the first steps towards becoming a saint when the Vatican announced that Pope Francis had authorised a decree declaring him “venerable”. Next up: beatification. Now at this stage you need to prove that the person had a life filled with heroic values, a saintly reputation and is responsible for one or two miracles along the way too (maybe curing tourists’ sore knees after traipsing up all the steps at Barcelona’s Park Güell?).

To be frank, you would have hoped that the creation of the Sagrada Família basilica, 144 years in the making, would have been enough of an endeavour to swing a sainthood. Because while this might be one of the most exclusive clubs in the world, surely there’s the potential to advance swiftly the occasional candidate? The Pope is perhaps mindful of the fact that, while Gaudí was an incredibly devout Catholic who remained single all his life and put his body through intense and lengthy fasts to display his commitment to God, he was, after all, an architect.

Now it’s not impossible, but it’s quite hard to be an architect and remain, well, saintly, at all times. Builders, meddling planners and ill-informed critics all tend to push these sensitive souls over the emotional edge every now and then. The esteemed writer on Catholicism Peter Stanford has indeed suggested that perhaps Gaudí is too complex and rich a figure to be moved along this particular conveyor belt. Sainthood, he said, “reflects an extraordinary life of religious devotion, and that clearly was a very important part of him, but it puts him in too small a box. In terms of people who could be in the biggest box possible or no box at all, Gaudí seems to me to be a very good example, because his imagination knew no boundaries.” There is also the question of whether Gaudí would have wanted this. Because someone upstairs was neglecting his needs when, in 1926, he was run over by a tram and killed while walking to church.

In the end, however, it matters little whether he is made an official saint, because people are already enraptured and mesmerised by his work, and make pilgrimages to see Casa Vicens and Casa Milà. And they can witness a true miracle: the Sagrada Família. “God’s architect” has already become a people’s saint.

items.titel: Democratic contenders are eyeing up the US presidential elections. Will Jon Ossoff be the party’s shining star?
items.anriss: For anyone hoping for a shot at the US presidency, the midterm elections are an excellent proving ground. There was one candidate this year who ticked all the boxes: Jon Ossoff, the incumbent Democratic senator from Georgia, who was the …

absaetze.t: Politics
November 11, 2026
3 Min Read
After big wins in the midterms, the Democrats are looking ahead to 2028. Georgia’s senator stands out as a potential answer to the inevitable question: who will run for president?

For anyone hoping for a shot at the US presidency, the midterm elections are an excellent proving ground. There was one candidate this year who ticked all the boxes: Jon Ossoff, the incumbent Democratic senator from Georgia, who was the party’s first victor of the night.

This allowed him to take to the stage early and give a thundering victory speech, which resembled those of the Obama era. Throughout the campaign, the telegenic 39-year-old was greeted like a rock star at rallies across the state, giving rousing speeches that tapped into voter concerns about the cost of living and alleged government cronyism.

Ossoff has attacked the self-enrichment that runs rampant through the Trump administration, which he calls “the Mar-a-Lago mafia” and the “Epstein elite”; he has found easy targets in the president’s ballroom project, his family businesses and more. While all Democrats running in the midterms tapped into concerns about the rising cost of living, Ossoff went for the jugular and claimed that people were getting poorer precisely because Donald Trump was getting richer.

His peak arguably came in August at a campaign rally in which he made a jab about Trump’s relationship with his loyal executive assistant, Natalie Harp. He suggested that the president would rather “travel with Natalie” than run the country – a reference to how Harp had accompanied him on an alternate plane after a potential threat against Air Force One at a Nato summit in July. It was a carefully worded taunt, short enough for social media and suggestive enough to send the internet into overdrive.

While Ossoff might just be edging into the wider public consciousness, he has been a rising star in the Democratic Party for some time. His messaging skills cut across the traditional political divides and he appeals to a broad tent of voters. Republicans had targeted Georgia – a purple state that swung from Joe Biden in 2020 to Trump in 2024 – as a potential midterm win. But Ossoff dominated the race and helped to carry Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms over the line.

Though Ossoff champions cost-of-living issues, he comes from a wealthy family. He was educated at a private school before attending Georgetown University and the London School of Economics. Early in his career, he worked in media and communications, before moving into politics with an unsuccessful House bid in 2017, followed by his Senate win in 2021.

As well as his charisma and sharp political instinct, the married father-of-two has another advantage: he straddles warring factions within the Democratic Party. As a millennial, he can appeal to younger voters and, while he is not aligned with the surging Democratic Socialist movement, he shares a lot of their messaging on big money. He is also Jewish but critical of Israel’s actions in Gaza, which means that he is well placed to try to bridge divides within the party over the issue.

The midterm win has now sent his reputation into the stratosphere and prediction markets currently put him as the favourite to win the 2028 election. Of course, a long road lies ahead and there will be a crowded field of strong Democratic contenders. So far, he has denied any plans to launch a presidential bid. But his actions tell a different story. The US can expect to be hearing a lot more from the silver-tongued senator.
